text.p: 1 London Nov 11 1731
Dear Momma

We take this opportunity to return you thanks for your kind letter, and are very glad to hear that sister July is so well recovered. Our cloths are very threadbare and look very shabby. We should be very glad to make them last till we come down to you at Christmas but they are worn out so already that we cannot. We have took several chances in the Lottery, and return you thanks for the money. I am, by one of the boys going away, now the eighth boy in the election, and shall, if I keep my place, I believe get into College, which I do not only hope to do, but also to get up higher. We have no particular news here. I hope you and sister Chichester and my sisters and little Miss Kitty are all very well. My brothers and I join in duty to you and love to sisters
This is all at present from
Your dutiful & affectionate son
Roger Newdigate
Mrs Webber gives her service to you and sisters.
2 Westminster March 11
Dear Momma

I received & would have answered yours before but being pretty much pressed in time & knowing your goodness would excuse me I deferred it till this opportunity. Mr Kollogrew sent an invitation to me & accordingly I waited on him on Tuesday last, He joins with his sister in service to you and all friends. I have according to your orders enquired about the Salmons & find that there are six parts in every volume, each part at one shilling a piece, & the binding will come to about one £ at least if you care to have them, Mr Barker desires one of the other volumes that they may be matched in the binding, & I dare say he won't impose on me.

My Lady Sadly & Sir Charles desires their services, I was at her house to dinner on Saturday last when she took me to the Opera, where I heard the famous Fannello, who I think (& you know I'm a great judge of music & a perfect master in the art of whistling) very well deserves his character & is the most extraordinary person I ever heard. You may think after the charms of his voice, how I shall bear the noise of rooks and the quawking of your Ladyship ducks, & the solitary walks near purling rills, with what you country ladies think so charming, the pleasing sonnets of the airy choir, which will appear to me, worse than the shrieking of a violin ill played on. I shall die to befoul my fingers with a filthy hoe & shall address your Ladyship in nothing but Italian now & Fannello's praises.
I hope you will excuse these airy flights which may seem odd to you but are common & fashionable and therefore necessary to us town gentlemen.
I am
Dear Momma
Your dutiful & affectionate son
R. Newdigate
Mrs Webber desires her service, I was going to thank you for the ale, but upon recollection I won't thank you till I have it.
Westminster November 15
Honoured Madam

I received yours & beg you would return Mr Bromley my acknowledgements of the favour he does me. I did not at first comprehend who was included in the name of Mr B... but having met with a clergyman who has for many years enjoyed the living of Buckington & has just got from our Chapter that of Hinckly (I have forgot his name). I was informed of the happy news of the visit intended to me & have been perplexing
myself ever since to find some way of avoiding it. I'm glad to hear Mr Chichester and my sister are safe arrived. I received on Wednesday last the Epitaph for my poor brother & think Mr Walwyn has with a great deal of elegance done justice to his character. I have just wrote to him to return him thanks. Imagining that you would have a curiosity to see it I have attempted it in English.
I will send a copy of the Latin one next week when I hear if you have any objections to it or not. I'll send it to Mr Rysbrack. I hope you'll excuse the hurry of this &
I remain
Your most affectionate & dutiful son
R Newdigate
For the Lady Newdigate, near Coventry, Warwickshire.
Calais August 21 New Stile

We set out from London, dear Madam, as we proposed, on Monday at two o'clock in a sloop of Mr Bonnets, and lay at anchor that night before Gravesend. Our cabins were very convenient and we slept as heartily, most of us, as if we were upon land. The next day we fell down to the Nor and saw 3 men of war riding there at anchor. From thence we came to the downs, leaving Goodwin Sands to the left hand. There were 3 more men of war there. We cast anchor here and lay that night, the wind for this part of the voyage being South East which was directly in our teeth.

The second morning we sailed within a league of Dover Castle, where we were becalmed and were obliged to cast anchor. The castle and cliff made a very beautiful appearance at that distance. Here we waited for the tide 3 hours. We were very fortunate in having a brisk gale upon weighing anchor which carried us in between 3 & 4 hours into this harbour, with the English and French coasts in our view all the way. We had a very agreeable voyage though not a very short one. We were 49 hours or thereabouts from the time we sat out. The voyage is sometimes performed in 24. There were none of the company at all sea sick.

Calais is a very neat, clean town, but nothing extraordinary. I think it exceeds all our seaports I have seen in the neatness of the streets, which is a sure sign of our exceeding them in our trade, for it is that which dirties our streets. The vast difference in the people, buildings, as well as the language makes it impossible for one to hesitate a minute whether we are in England, besides the crucifixes, one of which is stuck up in every opening about the town.

We went to see the church, which is a good old gothic building and was built by the English when they were masters of the town. The pictures are but indifferent and some of the altars most tawdrily dressed up with made flowers and garlands.

We are got in a very good inn here. The butler is exceeding bad but the Burgundy makes up for it. It is a very ridiculous sight to us that are not used to it to see the lowest of the workmen in their bags, solitares, and pig-tails. Here is a carpenter working at a chaise in the yard at this instant with a tail tied up in coarse brown tape that reaches several inches below his Bottom - .

Since I began we have agreed for our chaises at 19 guineas each. We have nothing now to do but to buy saddles and jack boots for the servants. We set out to morrow for Bologna in our way to Paris, which we hope to reach in three days.
Lord Litchfield, Sir Francis Dashwood and Jack go to morrow to see Dunkirk and on Saturday set sail from thence for England.

We are just come from seeing a monastery of Poor Clares, and a House of the Capuchins who are the dirtiest fellows I ever yet saw. They never touch money, but without any hindrance conducted us to a sister who received the money for them that we gave. You may give them as much money as you please, though they themselves are so scrupulous they won't handle a farthing of it from you. This is certainly a very ridiculous piece of form.

I have sent you a small piece of work of the Poor Clares to wear in your watch. You may see I have sent you a very particular account of our voyage, with many trifling circumstances that attend it, which I know you will receive with greater regard to the sender than the things themselves, or I should not have troubled you with this long detail. I shall be very glad to hear from you, Dear Madam, as soon as you please, to know how things go on in old England.

text.p: Daniel, as we imagined, is very awkward here, neither understands nor is understood, he will be still worse when he gets further, but I fancy he will do pretty well. My duty attends you and my best respects to Mr Ludford and family and all friends & Mr Chichester etc A. Palmer etc etc. I shall receive your letter as soon as it arrives there from Paris. Jack desires his service, and also the rest of our company. I have nothing to add but that I continue with the greatest affection
Your most dutiful son
R. Newdigate.

Angers Sept. 8th N.S.
Dear Madam
I have been for some time in hopes of receiving letters from England, but have yet received none. I am in expectation of them every day.

In my last I gave you an account of our journey to Paris. We stayed
there a week & left it on Monday the 1st New Style. We were almost entirely taken up with fitting ourselves out with necessaries and conveniences, & found it much of the same nature with London, a perfect vuide bourse as the French call it. I had the satisfaction of finding my clothes in the top of the fashion, so saved the expenses of making any alterations. Mr Waters came to wait upon us, to give us the form of drawing upon him when we have occasion.

We went to wait upon Lord Waldegrave. He was exceeding civil, sent his Gentleman of the Horse with us to show us Versailles, Marli etc and invited us to dinner. We dined then and met a great many English, but none of distinction, except the illustrious Colley Cibber , Poet Laureate. The day before we came away we were at his chapel, Lady Vane was there. She looked very gay, was very gently dressed, and painted a la mode francoise , the purest vermilion. I was surprised to find young Massingberd there & had only time to ask him how he did. We saw no other English there that we knew.

The town itself has a quite different air from London. The buildings are entirely stone & most of the houses of a prodigious height & all the streets extremely narrow. The River Seine very little exceeds our Fleet Ditch, though of infinite advantage to the town. The streets are all finely paved, like Whitehall, & the manner of hanging the lamps in the middle of the street by ropes from house to house, has a very pretty effect, though we did not see them lighted. The Berlin coaches are very easy and calculated for the narrowness of the streets, for they turned in a very small compass.

We saw the Palace of Luxembourg & the Gallery of Rubens, the History of Mary de Medicis. The prints I have at Arbury are extremely well taken and all the likenesses of the faces well preserved. The Dowager Queen of Spain at present inhabits it. The Tuilleries is a very old building and the Louvre not finished. We were at an opera. I had bad taste enough to think it the greatest jumble of noise and jargon that I ever yet heard, though they are certainly to be commended in one thing; that it is all their own manufacture without any foreign importation.

We had only time to run over Versailles It is certainly the greatest piece of magnificence since the time of Solomon, and all its grandeur owing to itself without any advantage of situation. The apartments lye all open to the meanest peasant, though the dirt they bring with them does not add much to the beauty of the place. The Great Gallery is the finest room I ever saw. It's entirely wainscoated with marble of different kinds, and adorned with antique statues set in niches. The ceiling is the history of the grand Monarch painted by Le Brun. In one of the rooms I saw the original picture of Darius's tent by the same hand.
You have Lens's copy of it by you which wants only the colouring, which is indeed the chief part.

The gardens are one vast profusion of expense. The quantity of marble in the fountains, statues and buildings, is immense. One would think there was no other stone in the country. We had not time to see half the garden & what we did see was to great disadvantage, the king being at Marli & none of the water works playing. From hence we went to Trianon, a little palace just by Versailles where the king used to retire from his grand apartments at that place. The apartments are very pretty but all unfurnished.

We came from thence to Marli, which is a most delightful place, as pretty as the other is magnificent. The ordinary waterworks all played. The whole scene put me in mind of the enchanted palaces of Romance. The account we have heard of it and used to mention agrees in every particular.

We arrived at Orleans on Tuesday night, and embarked our chaises there & fell down the river Loire to Blois. It is reckoned the finest river in France and is navigable for 440 miles, from Nantes to Roan. For the whole summer it is but just passable with the lightest boats, full of sand banks and very little water. In winter it is very large & troublesome. There is a prodigious bank raised all along the side to preserve the country from being ruined by it. It's a continual expense to keep it in repair and there is a fund set apart for that purpose.

At Blois we disembarked, heartily tired with the tediousness of our voyage, there being no other method of getting down but being pushed with poles. We lay the next night at Tours & the next arrived at this place. The whole road was very pleasant lying all along the raised bank of the river.

The town of Angers is very indifferent. We are got into a very good house, at the rate of about £3.10.0 per month apiece for our board, which is dear but the usual price. We have the house to ourselves. We came here on Saturday and yesterday received the visits of most of the English in the place. Lord Charles Manners, Lord Fitzwilliams, Mr Foster, Mr Read, Mr Wright & others that I knew nothing of. I fancy we shall find the place agreeable when we come to be acqainted with it.
We took a walk into the Manege yesterday. I saw Mr Bromley's and Sir Thomas Twysden arms up there which is the custom when people go away.
I hope you'll excuse the hurry of my letters. I am willing to send as much as I can, which makes me take no pains about the correctness of the stile.

I long very much to hear from you, which is the greatest pleasure I can receive at this distance. Till then I must content myself with the thoughts of old England and those I left in it, & believe my affection will grow, if
possible, more strong by absence. I have seen nothing hitherto, I assure you, but what has increased my esteem for my own country, nor one particular in which my judgement will give the preference to France. The misery of the poor & the extravagant profusion of the rich, for whom they labour is prodigious, though they are still happy for they think themselves so & know no better. For the last hundred miles we came even wooden shoes were finery, and most of the peasants we saw, men, women & children, had neither shoes nor stockings of any kind.
In my next I will send you an account of our sojournment here where we are encamped for the winter in very comfortable lodgings.
I am dearest Madam
Your most dutiful & most affectionate son
R Newdigate
A` Monsieur le Chevalier Newdigate a`Angers par Paris

I need not tell you, Dearest Madam, that I have succeeded, for you have on the outside the visible marks. This has been a day of considerable fatigue, but I have mended so much ever since I came here, & my spirits have been so well supported, that I do not find myself in the least the worse.

There was an appearance for me (I am assured, for I could not see) of 1500 freeholders, & not one voice against me. To see myself at once established in so creditable a manner you will easily imagine gives me very great pleasure; & the expense which is very considerable may, I hope, be made up before long by a prudent management.

Dick has been very obliging, but I should be glad if Clarke could send muster me up fifty or more & send a note payable at a short date to me at Mr Cooks, for I believe I must make a few visits before I see you.
I am, dearest Madam
Your affectionate & most dutiful Son
R N
December 22nd 1745

I was very much mortified... to break off my last like the Bear & the Fiddle, but the Fates & the Bellman would have it so. My hurry was so great that I don't know what I wrote, or where to begin. We thought it fair to give Mrs Barradel notice of our journey & she accordingly sent to us Mr Nichols, of Hillingdon, who is her first cousin & heir, to accompany us.

I set out at eleven from your brother's (on Sunday) in a chariot & four but when I came to L...s we sent it back for a coach & six, in which we left Town before two & got last night to Godstone. Our company consisted of L..., myself, Mr Nichols , & poor old Thomas, who moves me very much. At five this morning we set out & bated at Grinstead & Uckfield, the roads very bad but much worse from thence, about twice as deep as the deepest slough to Cotton Church, but no ways dangerous.

We were at a non plus at Lord Gage's park gate, no keeper to be found & our daylight near spent & the common road impossible. But under the sanction of my privilege we broke the chain & went through a charming park, a winding pool of a very great length, loosing itself in several branches amongst fine young woods. The soil however is bad & the park too flat. From hence we came into a chase of the Duke of Dorset's called the Broil, where we were really embroiled, for nothing could be deeper except a farm which we were so happy as to obtain leave to trespass over. But they had not the conscience to wait for our money.

From hence we mounted the Downs, where we were not so unreasonable as to load our horses but trudged to the top of them, & so far outstep'd them that we got to Lewes before them, above two miles & half. From the top of the Cliff Hill we saw the whole beautiful vale you admired all under water, & entered the town the opposite side, to what you did.

We called upon Trayton, whom we had given the trouble of sealing up everything. He is positive there is no will, for before Dick's last journey to Town he asked him if he had one, to which he answered he had not, but believed he must make one when he was in Town .. There has been no will found in Town, though not
absolutely certain there is none. It was a little melancholy to come to this desolate house, to be welcomed with mourning faces, as if coming to put an end to a scene of comfort & tranquillity which all enjoyed before, & in a place where I was so lately & so cheerfully entertained.

We are to do nothing to night but to morrow, between nine & ten, we are to make a general search. Mr Trayton, Mr Ridout & Mr Gilbert, a person engaged for Mr Bromfield, are to be with us. If I find upon the estimate any part of the goods, linen etc, are bargains I will endeavour to get them as part of my debt to Harefield from him, but if I am administrator I shall be able to choose upon those conditions. I have now a writing table in my view, which puts me in mind of your closet, but I don't want any ...
Spring Gardens 10 O'clock May the 9th 1747 Dear Sir

Enclosed I have sent you the daily Advertiser in which Sir Hugh avows your meeting, as this may occasion difference of sentiments in gentlemen. I will endeavour to fix the meeting we proposd as soon as possible & will make it my business today to find them out.

As the advertisement carries an insinuation that we have jointly asked votes, I believe you will think I ought to set that clear by declaring in answer that I never thought of addressing myself to anybody till Sir Hugh declared (as you heard) that he had asked the gentlemen and 5 or 600 freeholders. That even then I had not asked for myself or any one else but only desired they would reserve themselves to the sense of a meeting. That I then assured Sir Hugh that as I would not join him so I would not join any one else, nor even think of standing myself without their concurrence, having been chosen myself upon the resolution of such a meeting & being desirous to support & keep undivided the old institutions of the County in the old way. If something to this purpose meets with their approbation, or you think anything more should be added, pray let me know.
Who am
Your etc etc
R N
You will see Mr Cooke today
May 26th 1747 Spring Gardens
Dear Sir

The contents of your letter gave us great pleasure as a strong conviction of what before we only hoped. I can't yet find that any considerable ground is got by the positive solicitations carried on, most people are well upon their guard & refuse to engage.
In the Chancery Office I am told not above three would promise which is a particular instance, as we have no reason to expect much more than a majority there for the County Interest.

Mr Child's advertisement gives great satisfaction & will make many people easy. I should have wrote before but intended to wait upon you, which cant be now till Thursday or Friday but as I cant fix either till I know when the Scotch bill return to us with the Lords amendments. I hope it will be no confirmation to you
I am
Your most obliged humble servant
R N
Harefield Place February 12th 1747
Dearest Madam

I need not say it is a great concern to us not to meet you here, but when we consider what your employment is, that you are paying the last kind office to a child you loved & who loved you, we are better pleased that you are absent. I am no ways surprised to find by yours that your present melancholy situation affects your spirits & we both most heartily wish it was in our power to endeavour to administer comfort where you are, but that is impossible yet, my affairs here & in Town being fixed so as they can't be altered.

And indeed I cannot write myself without feeling for her, for you & all her family, though the difference in our ages & the distance of our lives gave less opportunity, yet I never met with anything from her, but an obliging behaviour & a sisterly affection, which I hope I shall always be so sensible of as not to omit any opportunity of doing service to those she leaves.

But the affection of all who love her must make them wish her pains at an end, her life has long been tiresome & without comfort, her situation full of danger & misery, which indeed she herself was least sensible of since the loss of him who occasioned it. In the sight of her friends no great one, but perhaps in some degree shortened her life. But from whencesoever it arose her strength has been impaired, her constitution broke, her spirits worn out, and the greatest blessing we can wish for her is the last, a contented & resigned end to a life which she has rather suffered than enjoyed.

Our comfort is, & her happiness will be, that she meant well & lived well, her children nearly come to that age when a mother's tenderness is often prejudicial, but never necessary as their proper education must be at a distance, & as to their affairs she was never capable of them. They were always, and will be, left in hands which she believes, & I hope, never will betray that trust. She will at once be free from pain and anguish, no longer tortured with physic & physicians, no longer a gaolkeeper trembling at every alarm; there the wicked cease from troubling, there the weary are at rest. In every light we see this change, it is for her advantage, & can anyone that loves her wish her to return to misery & sorrow.

I know you don't wish it for her. You are too well acquainted with her situation & constitution, & yet I do not wonder that your fortitude of mind is overcome & shaken in the tender office you are now performing, but I know you never forget that tears, like leaves which winter or tempest forces from the tree & scatters through the air, may flow at liberty over the tombs of the dead, but the stock & branches still remain firm & uninjurde & time again heals every wound.

But though we don't complain at your concern we are too much interested in your welfare not to wish it may be moderate, not too great nor too lasting. Your health is not established to bear it & when we think of you we should be happier if it was not necessary for you to be present, but this is unreasonable since in that hour such a friend is the greatest of blessings. The subject is to melancholy to dwell longer on & I should not have done it so long, but where you are I know it is unavoidable to you.

If nothing alters our route we propose to be in Town on Sunday night, to stay there till Thursday & on Friday, if you are still at Abinger to come there, if not to Harefield, but our purpose may be changed as there is occasion, except only that I must be in Town till Tuesday noon. If any alteration should be, as it is impossible for me to send either servant or horse, I beg you will send back to us here the messenger you have now sent. We shall not set out for Town till after dinner & shall be very anxious to know how you are.
My wife is writing for herself so I shall only add that I am
Dearest Madam
Your most affectionate, most dutiful son
R Newdigate
April 25 1748
Dear Sir

I am always glad when it is in my power to contribute to your pleasure, & happy in an opportunity of showing how much it is my wish to continue the union & friendship between our familys, which becomes relations & neighbours. As to your accounts between us they will be easily settled if I have the good luck to meet you at Harefield the week after next,

As to the disappointments you mention I assure you I hardly ever had your success in life from which I have reaped so entire a satisfaction, without my public employment. I have got rid of all the fatigue, all the mortification that attends the fruitless endeavours to serve ones country & can now enjoy my self without anyone's having a right to reproach me, & find so many sweets in that enjoyment that it will be no common temptation in my present way of thinking that will draw me out to sea again.
My wife etc etc
R N
Oxford Investiture 1749
My dearest Child
I am just stolen away from the side table where Thomas Rowney presides to give you an account of myself.

I got to Ladbrook sooner than expected, found Charles Palmer but indifferent, drank tea with Miss Betty, set out at 7 next morning, got to Great Tu, within five miles of Ditchley, where I luckily dined, for Lord Lichfield was gone 3 hours before I came there, so I was forced to come on.

At Thomas Rowney's found him, the Duke of Beauford etc talking over degrees. They determined that I should be a Doctor, which is to be performed tomorrow. This day I am only a Master & a nobleman. Lord Harley, Sir J Phillips, Sir J Shaw, Mr Drake, Mr Powney, Mr Wills, Mr Palmer and Mr Norb Berkely were dubbed Doctors of Civil Law; Mr Bagot, the old gentleman, & Mr Gibbs, architect, Masters of Arts. This was all we did today. We are now going to the Oratorio of Esther, which will cut this short. Tomorrow Lord Westmoreland, Sir Francis Dashwood, Sir L Holte, Lord Burleigh, myself & others are to have the honour.

The Orator is hard drove for speeches. The chief matter he takes from the Baronetage & Peerage . Tomorrow is the grand solemnity. Sir Watkin Win & Sir Wat B... are not yet come. Bagot tells me there is a scheme for his travelling with Lord Bruce, who is here, & his tutor, a gentleman who has been abroad. This gives me great joy. Lord Lichfield , who is the same boy in his robes, Doctor's gown or anything else, always jolly & good humoured, talks of going home on Friday. If so I shall go with him & stay part of the day. When I shall see thy dear face again I can't positively say. If I can get to Ladbrook on Saturday you will see me on Sunday, but I don't believe Lord Lichfield will go on Friday as he says. If so I shall not get home till Monday or Tuesday. You see, you must not expect me ... I begin already to think it long since I saw you. I begin already to think it long since I saw you.
Every body thinks this affair ill concerted. It would have been put off a month, but for Lady Williams, so that has turned out just wrong.
God Almighty bless & keep you, dear child ...
I have stolen a minute & must return, so good night. Think of me all day long & dream of me all night.
Yours most entirely
R N
Wednesday. 2 minutes before the Oratorio begins, 4 o'clock. I have not time to read what I have wrote.
Arbury April 26th 1749
Dear Sir

I thank you for the obliging manner in which you have taken the preference I have given you. I thought it due to so good a neighbour to give him an oppurtunity to make a situation which he likes still more agreeable, & it is very fortunate that the very lands which he would choose are those which are most to my purpose to part with. I am very glad my convenience, my motive for the offers, falls in so luckily with yours. The complaint is very trifling & you are very good to consider as an obligation what is really my interest.

To your objections I must answer, as Mr Eyre probably has, by my direction, that Mat Fields Farm may, as you say, very probably be untenanted. It was once so within the last 30 years for 3 years together which has indeed bust its reputation, but when the number of acres is considered must be worth the rent which has never been raised since I have had an account of it. You are misinformed as to Bayhurst grounds. They always went at £15 & might still have been let at the same rent if I had chose to add them to the distant farm which they used to lay to before. Fr. Trevor, I believe, will be glad to continue the tenant. The other two, as you say, will probably be empty, & I have no objection to making a reasonable deduction for that hazard.
You have not yet gone through half the falls of the old Park Wood and they all very unequal. The Mayhurst is as big again. I find a deduction of half the profits of the woods since I let it to you.

Mr Ware's farm was, as you say, advanced upon the building the house etc. It is now in very good repair & well tenanted, 7 or 8 years of a lease remaining, and a new lease desired at the same rent for as many years as I will grant it. You will not wonder, then, that I refuse to make any abatement with this particular. I will rather except it from the proposal than submit to any.
The present tenant of the Chalk Dell will, I believe, take a lease at the current rent.

The part of widow Townleys which I propose to sell is - 30 acres 3 roods 37 perches in extent . The remainder, without the house barns, stables, hovels etc is - 44.3.4. The yearly rent £55. I should not think the house an encumbrance if it stood on my part, & while you consider what you make of the tithe barn I believe you will allow the division
pretty equal. I am more unwilling to part with this than any of the land proposed, so can't think of selling the whole, & indeed our lands will be better divided thus than as now, or if you had the whole.

One great end I propose is to prevent our tenants interfering. The meadows which I reserve are the inlet of water to all my floated meadows & the rest lies convenient for my other farms. I tell you my reasons, without reserve, for the division as in the particular which I hope you will be satisfied with as you say it is not very material to you. I never heard of any repairs wanting, having laid out a considerable sum upon the farm within these 4 years.
In asking only 12 years purchase I think I have made considerable allowances for Dobyns house, which is now in good repair.

The valuation of the timber, I am assured, is made as usual in these cases but I don't understand it myself. There is no mistake in the valuation of the lands in the woods, - I mean the reserved right of the growth of timber. You now pay £20 for the underwood of the old Park Wood only, the tenants with their farms have the privilege of that of the little woods & shows the whole amounting to near 70 acres, one half of the value of which at least is, & has been always, in my own hands, & is worth more than a farm of £30 a year. Were the old Park Wood only stripped of the timber would you let it for £20 a year? & the young timber continuing to grow is worth a great deal more than the underwood would advance - more than no timber. Whatever reason there may be for disputing the valuation there can be none for setting it aside.

I have now examined all the objections & pointed out such parts as may admit of some abatement, but I am sorry to find we so widely differ that I can't venture to propose any, as there is only room for an inconsiderable one. For taking away that part of widow Townleys which you have added, & in the room of it adding the article which you have omitted, there is still near a £1000 difference between us.

I am not willing to leave out the lands you mention. My reason for offering them is that they are outskirts & lie more inconveniently to me than they do to you. I will give you no more trouble than only to take notice that this estate for above 40 years has held up its head under a greater burden than which now lies upon it. My predecessors submitted to receive nothing from it rather than dismember it & I thank God none of them had less reason to sell them than I have, & am therefore determined to sell it well or not at all.
You are very welcome to see any of the particulars, & if you desire further satisfaction in any particular I shall be very glad to wait upon you at the Courts on the 12th or after.

The Ladies all join in compliments to you & Mrs Cooke, my mother in
part for thinking of her love
I have ordered R Miles to fell what elms you desire
And am, Dear Sir
Etc
Arbury June 15th 1749
Dear Sir

I am sorry I did not express myself clearly enough to you at Harfield, to leave no doubt of my resolution as to the parcels which I shall sell, but hope you will not take it ill that after having reconsidered what I had before, upon full consideration, determined, I must repeat to you that I
cannot think of parting with more of Trenleys Farm than what is already in the particular.

Upon weighing the objections which you make to that particular I am convinced that they ought to have some force, and in consideration of some articles which do now appear to me overstraind, in consideration of your advanced offer and to show that I scorn to make an unreasonable advantage, I will abate £500 of my demand and am willing to take £9500 for the whole as in the particular given in.
As it is now time to enter upon the management of the lands which will be upon my hands in case we should not agree, I must beg the favour of an answer as soon as conveniently may be,
I am, Dear Sir
Your most faithful & obliged Cousin & humble servant
R N
Arbury February 12th 1749
Dear Sir

I have indeed neither thoughts nor desires to enter again into public life, and most heartily wish you success in your present undertaking. It is impossible for me to attend the meeting on Thursday at so short a warning but I will certainly wait upon you at Brentford in case of an opposition, and in the meantime, as you desire, will make applications to my friends in your favour, though I think it unnecessary as all those are, I am convinced, already prejudiced in your favour, who are capable of concern to see the County of Middlesex degraded into a mere Court Borough.

I am sorry that this reproach could ever have been laid upon it, but flatter myself, from the late exertion of liberty in Westminster, that you have reason to entertain better hopes, and that the eyes of men are open to distinguish between those who court their favours, with design to sell them
for honours & profit, and those who desire no other reward for their time, labour & expense than the satisfaction of having served them diligently, faithfully and disinterestedly.

I speak with a freedom that my present situation allows, and heartily wish every freeholder may be of the same sentiment with me, that in choosing you we lay an honourable burden upon you only to serve ourselves.
The ladies join me in compliments to yourself and Mrs Cooke, and in wishing you success without trouble.
I am, Dear Sir
Your affectionate cousin etc
R N
Dear Sir

I give you many thanks for your most obliging letter but indeed no fresh instance was necessary to convince me of your friendship. I must also beg you to express my gratitude to Dr Blackstone & Mrs Clitherow for their good opinion of me & endeavours to serve me.

When the County of Middlesex did me the honour to elect me, in which I hope I shall never forget my obligations to you, I was glad to know Parliament & ambitious to serve them. When they rejected me my concern was for the old County Interest which I at once broken & ruined. Since that time I have lived in more ease & tranquillity than ever I knew before, & it must be a great temptation indeed, no less an honour, that which you & my friends are now troubling yourselves to advance me to, which would prevail with me, circumstanced as I am, to enter again in public life. If that honour can admit of any advancement it is the manner in which my friends endeavour to obtain it for me, for which they have my acknowledgements, & I assure them that as I have been ignorant hitherto of every circumstance relative to this affair I will still continue so, & shall not presume to hear any overtures whatsoever for I have no pretensions, no determination whatever but to be sensible of the honour they have done me in their thoughts of me, & to be very well satisfied whatever is their conclusion. I must only beg that...

I must repeat my obligations to Dr Blackstone for his friendship to me, who have no title to it, & to yourself & Mrs Clitherow for your congratulations upon the appearance of success, so far beyond my expectations
or desires, Also for your account of what is going forward & I hope you will continue your correspondence.

What is the inducem't for moving a certain person into the upper house before his time? They will not upon my account run the hazard of dividing the Interest. I am ambitious of the honour of serving them but more so of the continuing that impregnable unanimity which has hitherto distinguished that University upon these occasions.
Mrs Clitherow & all your family have all our best wishes at all seasons
I am Dear Sir
Your most faithful & obliged humble servant
R N
Epping Place March 18th 1750
Dear Madam
I have very little to say in my defence for not writing to you sooner but as I know Sophie communicates to you the contents of my letters I hope you excuse it.

I received the enclosed yesterday by an express to Epping Place. I was not surprised at the contents of which I had heard a report, & well knew that whenever they were in a situation to want my assistance their pride would stoop to ask it. I have sent you my sister's letter & Mr Craven's with the answers &, as much as I can recollect of the contents of Mr Ludford's to Mr Craven.

The effects of a Commission taken out against Lord Donegall I have long ago considered. My sentiments upon that head stirred up the wrath of Mr Ludford long ago, as you may remember in one of his letters which I have at Arbury. I believe it to be the only certain method to secure to the children a vast inheritance in future & the share they are by law entitled to of the profits of the estate in the meantime, to be the only sure guard against the plundering them (if he should fall into bad hands) of the last, & against the marrying to some person who would take care to produce children to strip them of the first.

The effects of such a Commission with a Retrospect I have also considered & must confess that, notwithstanding the resentment which I can't deny the usage I have met with raises in me, I cannot consider it without concern & uneasiness. Mr Ludford must produce an account not only of what has come into his hands but of what Mr Chichester squandered, & answer it as far as the Executorship of the last will do so, & as far as his own abilities. Should it turn out that £2000 only, more than he can show to be laid up for the children, should be required of him, where will he go for that sum only? His estate is settled, he can't touch it, his personal estate though he strips to his shirt will not answer it. What then must be the consequence? Instead of 2000 perhaps he may have ten times that sum to answer for. How can he stand it? If this is the case, as it appears to me to be, should a Commission be obtained in an hostile manner. It is not a time to think of past injuries, nor even whether the sums which disappeared have been squandered in riot, extravagance & ambitious views, whether I have really known affectionate sisters, or any other tie but that of blood, but to consider that tie only, to consider two innocent nephews on one side, two helpless nieces on the other & as far as their interests are compatible to serve them all as well as I can.

In this view I have talked with all the gentlemen mentioned who will, I dare say, cooperate with me in any scheme that will prevent what Mr Ludford (inconsiderately if he really means it) says he does not fear, a Retrospect, but to make any proposals of accommodation to Lady Barrimore to stop the issuing of the Commission, or to do anything whatever to that end, I absolutely refuse, for the reasons above. For I can never consent to leave the inheritance of those nephews one moment in hazard, such as they are now in, & I have above represented.

I have desired F. Newdigate, if he finds by Lady Barrymore's Agent, whom he is to meet today, that I can be of any service as to the preventing the Retrospect, to give me notice, otherwise that it is better for Mr Ludford not to call me in, for if I am asked my sentiments as to the good of the family by Lady Barrimore I should not choose to answer, which would be enough to make her guess the reason & summon me before the Chancellor where I could not refuse to do so.

Tuesday the 19th. I have not seen Francis Newdigate but hear that Lady Barrimore is willing to treat but insists upon their producing his Lordship. It is upon Deal's affidavit that the Petition is founded. Mr Ludford now feels the imprudence of following the dictates of revenge & malice. I apprehend too he will suffer for his last folly at Warwick, which I fear has made him many powerful enemies who will push him to the utmost. Mr Stratford, who called upon me this morning, says the Attorney General, whom they understood to be retained in general for them, declares himself for Lady Barrimore. Wilbraham, too, is engaged on her side & a Mr Dickson is her Agent. No one but Mr Ludford seems to believe Lord Donegall can go through an examination & that a Commission will not pass. For my part I think & hope it will not fail, & only wish Mr Ludford may be wise enough to throw no difficulties in the way in case they can be prevailed upon to give up the Retrospect, which I should think they will, as Lord Barrimore himself had once the plucking of this pullet.
I propose to go to Harfield on Saturday in order to settle yours as well as my own affairs of which I will, at my return, give you an account. I rejoice to hear you are all well & am
Dearest Madam
Your most dutiful & affectionate son
R Newdigate
Park Place February 2nd 1752
Dear Madam,

I sent you an account last post which I doubt not will make you anxious to hear further. This morning I received a letter from Mr Dixon to desire me to meet him at Mr Wilbraham's who had much to say to me. I declined this, being really engaged, but if I had gone, Mr Wilbraham's arguments, I knew, could only regard his client, Lady Barrimore, for whom I am not concerned. Mr Dixon, by my appointment, however, has just brought me his sentiments which, he says, are that the method proposed & insisted upon by the Lord Chief Justice, to draw the bill simply and purely to give a power to let leases for 99 years, which is the end proposed, will not do, for that method will condemn the Deed of Trust, the Decree, the Council that advised it & all their proceedings upon it. This I told him is of no concern to me. If they think proper to act under it, they do it at their peril, but for my part I will never consent to a confirmation of them. He added that uses must be appointed for the money arising, & that there never was a case giving the surplus to the next of kin during a man's life, nor ever could be.

My proposal was to give a power to Trustees to let leases, & to apply the money arising from the estate, first, to the maintenance of Lord Donegall, secondly, to the payments of the debts, thirdly to be placed in Funds, to be distributed after the death of Lord Donegall to the next of kin by name, to Lady Barrimore, Lord Mazarine, & Arthur & John Chichester by name, or their legal representatives. This is necessary in the last case particularly, for otherwise Miss Chichester will have a share. He could not pretend this was not such a disposition as any man might legally make, and resorted at last to his directions which, he said, were very different, & he must have fresh instructions, which would make it impossible to obtain an account this Sessions.

I told him I should not object to such a bill as above, nor should object to a confirmation by Act of Parliament of such a deed as I could consent to, & that such a deed might have been drawn last year if others of the children's friends had been consulted. He said he understood I had refused to act or interfere. I told him my reason for it, that my sister's will had put it out of my power to act with Mr Ludford upon an equal footing but that I never had nor would refuse it where I could do them
service. The result of our conference was to let alone the Act of Parliament this Sessions & to endeavour to settle the whole in such a manner as I & my Council can approve, in order to have it confirmed by Parliament afterwards.

Thus ended the affair, & I am excused waiting upon the Lord Chancellor tomorrow. Mr Dixon owned the deed was drawn in too much haste but that Ludford had done such things & had such influence that it was not proper Lord Donegall should continue a minute longer in his hands. He could not say he had done & undone for his own interest, by which I perceived he meant the wills which had been made. That Ludford was exceedingly frightened, begged him not to be hard upon him & that he could have had him upon his knees if he pleased, the night before the inspection. But after that, in Court, his looks were changed & he would hardly pull his hat to him. But that at last he pressed hard to kept Lord Donegall, offered to keep him for a thousand a year only for, says Dixon, he had great schemes in his head. He was to oppose Lord B at Warwick!

The consequences of this whole, I hope & expect, will be greatly for the advantage of the children. This affair having been canvassed thus, they will probably not venture to act under a deed so impeached - if not, another must be drawn which I shall not approve unless the interest of the children is fully provided for & all the savings possible made. Thus, probably, Mr Ludford's Castle in the Air' will vanish, his £2000 is not paid, & perhaps never will, his accounts will be examined for the whole time Lord Donegall was with him, & the balance exacted. It is but justice it should be so, & if that is not done they are liable to be called to a strict account. A Commission may still pass, & all their deeds voided, & payments to be refunded.

We were in hopes of a letter from you last post but conclude you are well as we have heard nothing to the contrary from Arbury. Sir Walter Bagot is come, so is Lord Guernsey, but I have not seen Sir John Cotton. I fear he's at the point of death in our neighbourhood. Our street is littered of & noises kept out as much as possible. He came out of the country two days ago & has been worse ever since.

W. Palmer & the two Chichesters dined with us on Sunday. I think I never saw boys more improved than the two last, the eldest quite sensible, ready & entertaining, & Dr Nichols says great things of his improvements. We could not but be pleased that notwithstanding all they must be sure to have heard all day long to our disadvantage they seemed highly pleased & glad to see us.
James has just brought word that Sir John Cotton is dead, between 5 & 6 this evening. We have lost the best piece of the old Patriot Rock.
I am
Dearest Madam
Your most dutiful & affectionate son
R N

TEI.text:
Dear Madam
Macartney is returned from Guildford & has brought five affidavits to support our Petition proving Lord Donegall's incapacity. We find every day more people willing to prove it. I am to go tomorrow morning to settle the Petition with Council which, I hope, will be delivered to the Lord Chancellor before night. I waited on Lady Tyrawley today as she is a near relation of the family & have the satisfaction to find that she, as well as all mankind besides, thinks I am doing an act of justice, & for the service of the children. I hear not a word on their side, only Lady Barrimore's people seem not so much against the Commission though I believe it is only outside, for all their schemes are already blown up by the impeaching of the credit of the Deed, & the Commission will put it out of the power of anyone to impose upon Lord Donegall.
If the Chancellor approves we shall have him up in less than a fortnight. Our facts are very strong & can be well proved, though no other evidence of Lord Donegall's incapacity is necessary than the very deed they would confirm; if there was more contained in it than that he gives himself up to
Lady Barrimore's custody for his life without a possibility of his leaving her, let her use him never so ill, & besides giving up his whole fortune to Trustees without leaving himself a single shilling for his pocket, & even under his hardest masters he used to be allowed a guinea per month.
Lady Primson I saw the day before yesterday. She is a zealous advocate for Ludford , who was with her in Town. I hear a reason suggested, that some of her relations will suffer by a retrospect, which makes the matter clear.
Mrs Drelincourt is very stout & well in appearance. The bell waits...
I am, dearest Madam,
Your most dutiful & affectionate son,
R Newdigate

text.p: Lincoln's Inn Fields April 14th 1752
Dear Madam

I am just come from Lincoln's Inn Hall where our cause has been opened but the Chancellor, being obliged to go to Council, we could not proceed, but are to do so on Friday evening at 6 o'clock. Mr Ludford put in an affidavit on Saturday accusing me & my wife both of an inclination to have Lord Donegall ourselves, and some some other dirty insinuations which I was, much against my will, obliged to answer, & think I have done it fully & with candour & truth, having left out several strong things which I well remember, & put in nothing but what I was assured was absolutely necessary.

I have the satisfaction to find my conduct impeached by none but the contrary party, all others rather blaming me for not applying sooner rather than for this application. Mr Ludford came in a great passion, would not return my bow but belched forth to me,
Baronet! Things are very bad between you and me'.

I replied that I was sorry for it, or to that effect. He said he could prove that I & my wife had consulted together about having my Lord, & he would prove it so that I could not deny it. I answered I had denied it & had sworn to that denial & that I defied his proofs.
What will become of the noble peer no one can say, but Mr Ludford's conduct appears in such a light that no one, not his own council, can defend him.
I am going to Copt Hall tonight & cannot, I fear, see you so soon as we proposed, but we must go through with it now we are engaged.
I am
Dearest Madam
Your most dutiful son
R Newdigate
Ebdell has put in a mean dirty affidavit to support Ludford.
Friday April 17th 1752
My Dearest

We are put off again to Wednesday evening which mortifies me exceedingly. It is now ten o'clock. The Chancellor begun before 7, Forester spoke and Blackstone, very short but well enough. The Solicitor General then opened on the other side & spoke very little, I thought, to the purpose. Their affidavits were then read, and then Mr Clarke spoke for them, then Wilbraham, who fairly owned the whole transaction & insisted that it was the best agreement could be made for the family. Mr York followed. Their arguments were chiefly, that a Commission would have, no one knows, what end consequences, and would destroy all my Lords acts, from his coming of age.

Then my affidavit was read, & Mr Ludfords answer, which I found on my coming here but which contradicts not one fact which I have advanced except that of the staircase, which he swears was not making, I think, till April. But I never said 'making', but 'altering', which was doing as I have sworn, & which you must well remember. Afterwards Mr Henley was going to reply when the Lord Chancellor broke up the Court & fixed Wednesday. He took away Ludfords letter, which I annexed to my affidavit, with him. He said the surplus was not provided for as it ought, & that that was a fault in their deed, & on going wished the parties could agree on some method to settle that. To which the Solicitor General answered that it had been considered as well as possible & nothing more could be done.

My Council all agree that there can be no agreement so we must wait the issue on Wednesday, which cannot fail to conclude, so consider before you come down what you will do. I think you had better set out on Monday & leave me, but you shall decide as you please,
I am tired so Adieu
My Dearest Sophie
Your most affectionate
R N
April 18th 1752 Lincoln's Inn Fields
Dear Madam

I have little more to say yet, our Affair not being concluded last night as I expected, but we are to have another hearing on Wednesday. The Chancellor sat upon us from before seven till past ten, heard all the affidavits & all the Council except Mr Henley, upon the reply for us. Their chief arguments against us were that, I was a stranger in blood to Lord Donegall, that all his relations were agreed, that Macartney had contradicted his evidence (for my Lord) of last year, that he was the instigator of this & was turned out because he could not account. One of their Council, Wilbraham, confessed my lord's weakness as fully as could be wished, & said that all had been done that could be in such a case by the Deed, to which the Chancellor himself answered that there was a flaw in the distribution of the surplus which is a declaration that gives one great satisfaction, as he has already shown by it that he thinks my application neither improper nor frivolous. He added that something must be done in it & advised all parties to consider of it against the next day.

I am going to Epping again and have some thoughts of sending the
coach off on Monday but shall leave the ladies to their choice. It is a great mortification to be kept from Arbury but I must content myself.
I am, dearest Madam
Your most affectionate & dutiful son
R Newdigate
Lincolns Inn April 23 1752
Dearest Madam

We have lost our cause, very much contrary to the expectation of every body that knew anything of it. The Chancellor spoke an hour & half & always mentioned me with honour, that I had applied properly, that I had applied worthily & honourably, but that Lord Donegall, being confessedly no idiot nor lunatic, it was in the sound discretion of the Court whether they would grant a Commission or not, & that no line being drawn, no time of commencement of insanity, a jury might find back to Lord Donegall's birth, which would set aside the marriage settlement of Lord Donegall, & that upon Mr Chichester, & therefore the infants would be in greater danger under a Commission than at present under the Deed. Therefore he dismissed the Petition. He said it might be proper still to enquire about £3720 which Mr Ludford released, & that belongs to little Jack, but I don't know how far I may think proper to proceed in this affair again.

I am very easy under this disappointment, having followed the opinion of Mr Fazakerley & the other Councils in the discharging what I thought my duty in order to save a great sum of money & a great inheritance to the two poor orphans, who are now liable not only to loose that whole sum but loose Lord Donegall's inheritance, & the inheritance even to Mr Chichester's estate too, if Lord Donegall is married & a child produced & a Lunacy should be obtained afterwards which nothing but a Commission, now granted, can effectually prevent. I have not totally lost my time or trouble or expense, for everyone is convinced my application was well grounded & disinterested, which is a very great satisfaction, for everyone agrees that I have acted the part I ought.
I shall return to Epping tomorrow & propose to set out for Arbury on Friday morning early, & hope to be there on Saturday night, & that we shall see you soon after,
I am Dearest Madam
Your most affectionate & dutiful son
R Newdigate
Thursday February 15th 1753
Dear Madam

I have only time to tell you I am just come from the Judges where I met Ludford & the rest. He seemed very quietly disposed & the rest rather fond than otherwise. By consent we put it off to try if anything can be done by the reference before Monday next.

Last Monday I myself proposed to Mr Barry, by a friend, to refer to Mr Fazakerley the whole matter, which Mr Barry accepted, & on Tuesday evening Mr Fazakerley expected Mr Wilbraham, their referee to meet him, but with him came the whole crew, which, not a little, nettled Fazakerley, who expected Wilbraham alone, & made him interrogate Ludford upon the deed which he destroyed till he looked as if he was ready to sink into the earth. He said the deed of 1746 which he burnt would have destroyed the family. Fazakerley took him up.
'And did you make such a deed, Sir?'

Mr Dixon came to me at the Coffee House, where I told him he deserved to be pulled by the nose for the letter he wrote about me. Some few words more passed but he was all along rather fond & fawning. What will be the issue? I cannot yet tell if they will leave their own referee & mine to themselves. It will be fairly & easily settled, & if they don't all mankind say it is impossible that their bill, as it is, should pass either House. Besides, I had an hint yesterday that their great friend, Lord Brooke, was concerned to have it thought he made a party matter of it. Said he should be glad to talk with me, & I shall go accordingly tomorrow or next day.
There seems to me great appearance of success but one way to be sure of it is to be in the right & then one can never want it
I am
Dearest Madam
Your most dutiful & affectionate son
R N
Dear Madam

Going yesterday morning to Mr Eyre's to consider of the hearing before the Lords on Friday, I found a letter from their Agent that as I had signified my intention to petition for a Commission he would not give the Lords any further trouble about the Bill but would put it off till that affair is determined. This he did for a fortnight, which is in effect dropping the Bill. Thus I have obtained a complete victory in the first attack, which I was always of opinion I should, for what I had to produce at the Bar is a deep laid dark scene of iniquity, which they contrived to shuffle off at the Committee but which would have hurt them much more at the Bar where the Chancellor is present, & for that reason they did not care to face us. As they have not totally dropped the Bill the Chancellor, I'm afraid, will not let me petition whilst the affair is in the House of Lords , which will put me to this inconvenience, that I cannot proceed till the Session is at an end. But as it is more for their interest than mine that the affair should be determined soon I hope something will be contrived to go on immediately & I have no more doubts of succeeding in the Commission than I had in putting an end to their Bill in the House of Lords .

Mr Ludford was with Mr Fazakerly on Monday & talked of referring the matter to him & Wilbraham. But I have nothing to refer. All mankind agree that a Commission is the only desirable thing. All mankind call upon me to do my utmost to obtain it. My honour is engaged for it, & justice requires that Lord Donegall's affairs should continue no longer in such hands.

Though Ludford is not the object of my concern yet his family is, & I am ready to save them where I can, consistently with honour & justice, but they have tried every art & the utmost their Court Friends could do for them, their new allies, Lords Brook & Archer, but thank God justice has prevailed there, & I doubt not will in the other, though Mr Ludford has declared he will oppose the Commission while I have it twenty times under his head is the best thing for the family. If he alone could suffer by a retrospect it is no more than he well deserves. From the proofs he has with him, & his behaviour since his breach with them last year, which he insists was only because the interests of the children were neglected, Macartney rises every day in our opinion & I greatly hope his future conduct will be agreeable to it. Deal, & a Mr Hill, who lived with Lady Donegall, & many others, are ready to make affidavits or do
anything to assist the children. We want no evidence, nor anything but a speedy hearing.
I am, dearest Madam
Your most dutiful & affectionate son
R Newdigate
Dear Madam

We had a meeting today at the Judges Chambers where they have positively refused (notwithstanding what they wrote as in the last), to submit to the award of Mr Fazakerley & Wilbraham, who fully agreed & called the attorneys to tell them the result as you heard before. They carried their assurance so far as to deny the fact, as you will soon be told in Warwickshire by one of the archcontrivers, though Mr Wilbraham their own referee declaring the clauses they refuse are the best thing that can be for the good of the family. So we are all at sea again & the opposition in the House of Lords must go on.

I am sorry for it, but the further they go the deeper they plunge, & the advantages I have obtained by the reference are very considerable, as all men must acknowledge that malice has nothing to do in my prosecution & that I have no other object but what I declare. I suppose their bill will be in the House of Lords to morrow where my Petition shall directly follow,
I am, Dear Madam
In great haste
Yours most dutifully
R N
Park Place March 17th 1753
Dear Madam

Just come from the Play & have not time to send you a long letter but only in short to say that I have great hopes that my Council in the Committee of Lords today have given their Bill a fatal stroke, at least that side wind confirmation of their proceedings, which was the reason of their bringing the Bill, for the leasing the Town of Belfast. I don't object.
The Committee came to no determination today but are to do so on Tuesday next, but by the looks of the Committee, & the long faces of my adversaries, I venture to promise myself success. They have chose to expose themselves, & they have had it to day strongly, particularly Mr Ludford. They would not agree to make an amicable end before, & they deserved it, & now they have put the affair on such a footing that it is impossible for me to let the confirmation of the deed pass with any modification they may offer, if the Lords should, as I persuade myself they will, strike out the deed from the Bill.

The whole scene of iniquity has been displayed, but it is so deep it requires much enquiry to know all its secret recesses, & that enquiry will come in the Court of Chancery. They may thank themselves for that too.
The Bell will not stay
I am Dearest Madam,
Your most dutiful & affectionate son
R Newdigate
