text.p: Park Place March 22nd 1753
Dear Madam

I have nothing more to send you in relation to the Donegall affair but that in order to clear myself from the imputation of having obstructed a public as well as a private benefit by the throwing out the Bill for leasing the town of Belfast, as in the Committee I had consented to their powers of leasing as fully as they asked them, if they would take them simply & without a confirmation of the Deed of 1751, but they refused unless upon their own conditions. I contrived yesterday to speak to the Lord Chancellor myself & to let him know I was willing & desirous the Bill might go on for the leasing the town, & if it was possible without Lord Donegall's assent, which I could not procure, would carry it on myself. He answered that I could not without his consent. Do they then obstruct the rebuilding of the town or do I?

The list sent you last post I find was faulty. Their 7 Lords were Lord
Sandys, who alone spoke for them, Lords Brooke, Archer, Hertford, Warwick (but I am not quite sure he voted), the Duke of Dorset & Lord Kildare. The 14 that voted for me were Lord Oxford, Lords Raymond, Marchmont, Finlater, who spoke, Lords Shaftesbury, Litchfield, Ward, Northampton, Folly, Aberdeen, Folkestone, Willoughby of Parham, Feversham & the Duke of Portland.

Ludford , I hear, says the Scotch Lords came down & that it was a contest between the Scotch & English linen manufacturers. That that is false appears from their being 3 Scotch Lords on one side & 3 Irish on the other, so that it was not carried by them. Those whom people call Court Lords on both sides were equal too, & all the Patriot Lords, thank God, were on mine.

The House of Lords have gained reputation by rejecting a Bill which, upon the face of it, is a job. I will not say a W...k job as some lords have done, but all do me the honour to clear me from all imputations, & truth breaks out in spite of all the fogs that the Devil & his abettors have raised.

Ludford, I find, is endeavouring to stir something against upon G.N's account but thank God the parties concerned are so satisfied that I will do them justice that he stands alone. I wish he could fall alone too, as by the answer he has put into my Bill he is likely to fall, & that his family may not suffer for him,
I am, Dearest Madam
Your most dutiful & affectionate son
R Newdigate

TEI.text:
November 13th 1760 Spring Gardens
My best & Dearest
On the other side I send you the great news of the day, for which the Park guns were fired this morning. The Guard fired volleys tonight & all the Town is bonfire & illumination.
I foolishly swore at the Post last night for not bringing me a letter from my Dear Sophie, but I was sure it had miscarried & that I shall hear tomorrow, which upon recollection is as soon as I can possibly do so , but my life has been so very rapid & contained such variety since I left you
that I have fancied much more time than 3 days has past.
In my last I told you I was to be presented the next morning. I was so, & we were all most graciously received & afterwards saw the University of Cambridge present their their Address. Today I was at the Drawing Room which was also much crowded. I never saw a greater propriety of behaviour upon all these occasions than in the young monarch, so obliging, so free, so easy, yet preserving a proper dignity throughout. At the Leve`e yesterday he spoke to all that were introduced, & today in the Drawing Room of some hundreds of ladies I believe he omitted none, & all with an ease & readiness as if he had been King all his life.
Yesterday the Vice Chancellor came up. We expect to be nobly attended tomorrow. I have been all day upon the prance in Lockwoods Coach to great men's doors to desire their attendance; Lord Granville's, Mr Pitts, Mr Legge's the Speaker etc. At all I was very graciously received. Mr Pitt, as Secretary of State, will attend in his Office. Mr Leg will put on the Doctor's gown. We are to walk in procession from St James's Coffee House & afterwards to go to the Princess.
The Duke of Beauford, Lord Abingdon, Suffolk, etc, are come up. The archbishops, Bishop of Durham, Duke of Leeds etc etc. Lord Litchfield is in Town but, alas, our Chancellor will not. Writes from Bath he can't bear a sudden journey & if he could, could not go through the fatigue. Tic a pity but we must make the best of it. P. Palmer is just come. He will go but dares not attempt to kneel. Mrs Prows is better. Lady Williams is come up in a great fright. Sir Watkyn Williams Wynn has had a milliary fever but they say is safe. I can see nobody but at Court where I pass all my time. Yesterday indeed I condescended to dine at Lockwoods. Your brother I have not seen, nor heard if he will come.
I had letters yesterday from Winchester. The 1st Division of L... come in today. Our first march tomorrow will be to Newbury in a day. On Wednesday I apprehend they will be at Shipston & Chipping Norton & halt Thursday. On one of those of days, I flatter myself, I shall join them & still march one division into the County. When I know more you shall hear it.
The copy of a letter from the King of Prussia to his Queen at Magdebourg, Tranquillises vous Madame, enfin j'ai battu Monsieur Dan, la Victoire est complette, je les ai bien raffle`s en peasant les ponts'.
Marshal Dan, with his left, occupied the strong camp near Torgau which Prince Henry, sometime since, held out against him. His right was covered with an abattoir de bois - trees felled, with cannon placed among them. The King ordered General Ziethen to attack the Marshal's left at eleven of clock which, after some resistance, he forced, upon which the
King attacked the right & carried it. The action was very bloody, there and in the trenches, but at last the rout was general. The King took all their cannon & turned it upon them, & made great slaughter of the enemy, who never fired again afterwards. The action lasted till 7 & the Prussians continud under arms upon the bridges till 10. Marshal Dan escaped over the Alb in a boat.

text.p: House of Commons January 25th 1761

I have just seen a Petition which Sergeant Hewitt will present tomorrow from the inhabitants of Coventry for a road from thence through Caresley, Corley, Fillongley, Slolely Hill, Whitacre, Bentley to Baddesley Coalpits & so to Tamworth. I have wrote to Mr Baxter to acquaint my neighbours of Atherstone, & desire you will do so to those at Nuneaton & the neighbourhood, particularly Mr Busleton, Mr Vincent & Mr Barber.

Some of the principal inhabitants of Corley & Fillongley declared to me their intention to oppose any such attempt, and if they will all agree to sign a Petition as oppressive to them, without hopes of any emolument, and the inhabitants of Atherstone & Nuneaton will sign another, as it must greatly affect both towns, and the present as well as the intended turnpike roads through them, and the mortgagees of the Hinkley Road & acting Commissioners will sign another (or, if thought more expedient all may join in one) to show that this new project is for a road parallel through out to one or the other of those roads, and if ever effected must hurt their tolls, and if measured cannot be more than one mile nearer to Baddesley & Birch Coppice pits than the road through Nuneaton & Atherstone I am
well assured the project will, without difficulty, be brought to an end. I desire you will also give notice of this to Mr Lines & Roger Roe, to acquaint the inhabitants of Corley & Fillongley.

Give my compliments to all and let them know I desire to have their opinions upon the subject, & if they think proper to oppose I am ready to give them my assistance, & desire to have an answer as soon as possible.

I send you enclosed a Petition which I received from Mr Baxter for the addition to be made to the new intended road from Atherstone etc which I think, with the amendments which I have made, will do very well if they think proper to approve and sign it, & let Mr Baxter or Mr Fowler send it to me. I will put it into Sir Charles Mordaunt's care.

I do not find my opinion altered by the argument which you are told to send me against an opposition to the Badgley bill, nor by what I have read in letters, nor can I see the Justice of the people of Atherstone or Nuneaton who, for their convenience, would load the people of Corley, Fillongley, & my own tenants at Astley with a unprofitable & intolerable burden, but I have not yet seen Mr Baxter, so can't yet say what I shall think necessary to be done.

You must take what the Astley tenants will pay you for Dr Winchester, & pay it Mr Fletcher when you get it, for I cannot get at the book, if I haven't got it , but I think I left it you out . If he has anything to say to the Doctor let him write, himself, don't you do it.

I am glad to hear you are at work in the garden again, for I will have no more carting after this spring. Do you keep the stag out still? I don't propose to quick any part of Thomas Jelliff's this year, but don't forget the nursery in New Orchard. Tell Roger Roe I think he had better cover his
sashes with oild paper till the inside is done, or, if not, all the lower panes as I don't choose to hazard the plate glass. Have you received the panes I ordered in lieu of the broken ones?

You give me no answer whether Cooper will be a Sergeant which I desired you to ask him? I am sorry for poor Uxbridge. I am afraid they use the horses very ill in taking them back, for I commonly now lose an horse or two by the journey. I am sorry for your colds.

As to cash to Mr Vincent it is so convenient a way of having my returns by taking the pay here in Town that you must contrive to supply him with pay for the men for the next month, let whatever will be the consequence. The whole pay, if the Company was complete, is about £50, which you may pay by 10 or £20, as he wants it, from this time to the 20th of March, & if you put off all other payments for that time. The men must be supplied, but I hope you will not be put to those difficulties.

My new tenants for Lord Coventry's land you should press, as well as all the rest in arrears. May I hope in that time it will not put you to distress. Sell the hogs you propose ... Keep the poles a little longer.

I am obliged to you all for your care & diligence in my cause, & very happy in the success of it, which I hope will tend to keep the rest of my neighbours from running to that vile shop of Law which can only conduct them to ruin. Preach this doctrine amongst them & let them know that it is not out of wrath to White but for the sake of example to others that I have given orders to proceed against him for the last penny, & I hope they will never forget this remarkable instance, that it is not out of goodwill or compassion to themselves but merely from the desire to injure me that they & their complaints are so well received there.

I think you will do well to get in some cattle to eat the grass but whether to buy them or to joist some in will turn to most advantage I am a little doubtful, but this I leave to your judgement, which must be directed by the price of the cattle.

I hope you have gone on peaceably & quickly with the tithe & that John Pain in particular has not been troublesome. I wrote to you last post & shall be glad to hear a particular account of your goings on.

I hope Francis is careful of his cellars & that you take care they are not always open, as when I am at home, for treating & junketing at this time are out of season, & I hope, & don't doubt, you will maintain the family at as little expense as possible.

My service to Mr Preston & all friends I have received of Robert Haymes, of Hurly 5 shillings and 6 pence for his wife. So you must pay it to Jee at the Swan Inn at Atherstone, where her husband orders her to go for it.
Arbury May 9th 1761
Dear Sir
I have given Mr Truesdales proposal the fullest consideration & shall send you my deliberate answer to every particular.

Though there are same lands which I should have been as well pleased if he had left yet I have no objection to those he has chosen for himself, & am willing to let him have the whole particular, in all £355 per annum as proposd & at the price proposd. I shall only observe that a considerable concession is made in allowing 20 shillings per acre for the meadows in Goodchilds Farm, which I reserve, when his whole farm is let, one with another, at 14 shillings only per acre, and that the meadows which I give up at his desire from Wingroves Farm, which he values at 20 shillings, is fairly worth 30 shillings per acre.

I cannot understand why Norris's is to be valud only at 14 years purchase, which I cannot submit to, as his orchard & garden are worth full two thirds of what the whole is valued at. I must therefore desire they may be reserved out of the sale.

In the room of Goodchilds Barn, which I reserve, I have given up that which is in my own hands & lies more convenient, which is used as a workshop. John Iv has barns enough without that at Moorhall, but if Mr
Truesdale is of another opinion he shall have liberty to remove it, but I will not be at one shilling charge on that head.
I am willing to make the usual allowance in the timber & in short to take £1000 for all that is growing on the premises.

Whether the purchase is concluded or not before the 1st of July I must desire £2000, in case we should agree, may be advanced to be made up to to £7000 on the conclusion, & will submit to take 4 only, though I pay at this time 5, & wait a reasonable time for the remainder.

I have now gone through the particulars of your letter & shall only observe that I am surprised to find no mention made of the Place house itself. Does Mr Truesdale mean that I shall pull it down & convert the materials myself? For I cannot believe he can expect that such an house, the materials of which alone were valued by your brother at £800, exclusive of half a mile of lead pipes from the conduit & ponds, should pass in silence in so trifling a sale as this, of £350 per annum . If he means the first I am ready to agree to it. If the last I must beg you will inform him that I look upon it as no favour done me in giving 30 years purchase for old rents, nor £1000 for £1350 worth of timbers; for what then am I to make of such a concession or improve upon myself in thinking I get 30 years purchase when I give back above two years purchase in the value of the mansion, which alone was let within these 20 years at £70 per annum .

Mr Wight has just left me & I desire you will inform Mr Palmer that I shall pay in £500 more to Lord Coventry at the beginning of next week. I have then but a small sum unprovided, which he assures me I may depend upon before the time, & having thus provided for my new purchase I am very easy whether I immediately dispose of Harefield or wait till a Peace, when I am sure to have no dispute for 30 years purchase, nor a considerable sum for an house capable of great improvement & whose situation & other conveniences will not fail to give them due value. I know as well as Mr Truesdale that this is a bad time to sell, & the worst consequence to me will be the continuing to pay for a short time 5 for the money.

But as in the beginning of our treaty I declared myself ready to abate something of my demand for the house, & that it may not go off, as from your letter I conclude it will, with the reputation of invincible obstinancy on my side, I desire you will tell him, as my last word, that I am ready to take for the whole £12 000, & nothing under. This is my fixed resolution.

I send you back the copy of your letter which came to me from Leicester (where I shall not return till Monday night) fearing you may
not have a copy. Did you receive mine on the death of Mrs Jones? I am much obligd to you for the great pains you have taken,
& I am, Dear Sir
Your most sincere friend & humble servant
R N
Arbury June 6th 1761
Dear Sir

I am very sensible that you are in the right & that I can afford to sell for at least £200 less this year than the next, & though in case of a Peace I might expect much more yet as that is uncertain I would not let Mr Truesdale go for a trifle. But he is surely the hardest man to deal with that ever was.

He now offers £11,550. Before, it was £11,542, a very great condescension! But does he mean it upon the terms of my letter & Norris's house & orchards, or will he let me carry away the worthless materials of the place? I have no answer to these. As to the barns at Moorhall I do absolutely insist upon their being reserved, & will not conclude without.

The Church (all but the pew below the Chancel & the gentlemens' seats), & churchyard must be specially excepted. The water must run as at present, & my tenants for Cositas & Venables must have their turns of the water. The timber we valued at £1350 when the stockings etc
were excepted, which amounts to £173, so I conclude it cannot be overvalued, & I have a right to insist upon that addition. But this you will represent, & do what you can. If the rest is agreed to I have only to put my proposal also in form which, if he rejects, - Farewell, Mr Truesdale.
I will then take the 11,000 guineas which he offers upon these conditions: -
1st. That upon my mother's signing the deeds he shall present her with one hundred guineas, which she insists upon for her right in the placehouse,
2nd. That he shall receive the rents from Lady Day last, & pay 4 for the purchase money from thence.
3rd. That he shall pay the arrears of rent due at Lady Day last on the 1st of July in the enclosed rent roll,
4th. That he shall also advance the £1500 on the first of July.

The payment of the remainder may be left to his & my convenience. Those sums for which I pay 5 cannot be repaid till the year is out; which will be in March - £4000, in April 1500, & if they will lower their interest may not be wanted then. Only he must undertake to enable me to give them notice. The sums of £1000 & £400, for which I pay the same, may be repaid as soon as I can receive them. But in those also I will allow some time if he requires it.

Mr Hoare's mortgage, I apprehend, must be paid on the exchange of the deeds. But if an article is signed, that may be put off till it suits him. As this will be much within the terms of payment which he himself offers I hope he will consider & make the rest easy to me. And particularly if it shall appear that there is such an error as the one above in calculating the timber, that he will then make an addition for it which is but just.

But in this, & what remains, I leave myself to your discretion, being well assured that you will do all you can for me. But pray do not forget that nothing but this encumbrance, brought on me by my new purchase, could make me consent to anything like the terms contained in this, & but for that Mr Truesdale or somebody else should pay for an hundred pleasures & conveniences that that place will afford to such a purchaser.
I will add no more but to desire that if he boggles at these I may hear no more of him.
I am,
Yours most sincerely

R N
Time is so short that I must have an immediate answer, & pray do what you can to secure me part of the £1500 (if he refuses this) elsewhere on any terms, for fear that Mr Wright should fail.
Arbury July 4th 1761
Dear Sir

I should have been very glad to have known upon what terms you have the money which you have paid for me, as it would be a real satisfaction to me to be assured you have put yourself to no inconvenience & I should better have known how to deal with that B... Mr Truesdale .

But no situation of my assessment shall bring me to submit to his new articles which, dictatorlike, he produces without scruple when he himself will not give way in one tittle. I will therefore be positive on my side.

First, I peremtorily declare I will not convey on any terms one inch of the Chancel or of Brackenbury Chapel, nor one yard of the churchyard.
Before, he only desired the use of them, which I am ready to agree to, as in my last.

2nd, I will not convey to him Goodchilds Barn, nor anything at Moorhall but the materials of J Eve's Barn. As I retain above 20 acres of Goodchilds Farm I will have that barn with them, as I give up a barn (the Workhouse) that lies more convenient for Goodchilds use.

3rd If by fixtures are meant marble tables in the Hall, brewing vessels, cooler, boilers etc, grates or such like, they all belong to my mother, & he will not have them unless he pays for them. I would not have stood on little things but he shows me the way.
As to the rest, the pipes, cisterns & the sole use of the conduit, & liberty to mend the pipes, doing no wilful damage to Richard Hills farm I agree to.

The great Pond near Ashleys. I will not on any terms convey the use of the water as far as the arch will carry it, for the use of the Place; & liberty to fix & repair sluices for that purpose he may have. The rest, with fish & fishing, I reserve to be let with the manors, & will not separate them.

I am in no hurry for the arrears, for all I desire is to have them secured, & as the tenants, however poor, are responsible I will stay as long as he pleases if he will covenant that they shall pay me in the first place & his growing rent after I am served. I don't choose to discount being unwilling, as he wont let me have another shilling from him, that he should ever get another from me.

Pray tell him it is too late now July 1st is over to enhance upon his demands, & if he does not choose the purchase under the terms above I desire that neither you nor I may have further trouble. I can depend upon Mr Wright in a short time, & if any particular day is necessary to refund you by I may know it so that I may press him farther. You are all my concern on this occasion.

As he does not pay till Michaelmas the receiving the rents till then is only a matter of course & not to my advantage at all. Prompt payment is certainly so. I should have added that he is welcome to use the house as he pleases, even before the articles are signed. The crop & the grass of the orchard etc till Michaelmas I must have or be paid for.
I send you the inventory. They are all of small value. If you agree they shall all go to Brackenbury unless he will pay for what he wants.
On Monday I go to to Leicester & propose to be back on Saturday. I forgot to thank you for your last which gave me great satisfaction & will send you some franks the first opportunity
&am

etc
You still say nothing whether he expects interest for the £1500 till Michaelmas. From his other exactness I conclude he does, & if so must pay it.
92 Arbury July 17th 1761
To Mr Eyre, Attorney Etc
Dear Sir

I have executed & return enclosed the Article with some small alterations, the first in relation to moving J. Eves Barn. I have given him to Lady Day, but if he desires to Midsummer I have no objection, but a time must be fixed, & Lady Day is long enough for pulling down & removing, as he re-erects upon his own premises. Goodchild, having the lease from me may, if he pleases, keep Venables & Costars till the end of his term, so I will not object to his having the barn, provided he gives it up with those meadows which, as it must be by an agreement with him, cannot hurt his landlord. I did not understand he was to have the oak that is felled this spring. It should in reason have been excepted as he has more timber already than he pays for.

I don't understand the words 'free use in common'. As to the pews they must be better explained in the deed, & I desire you will now explain my sense of them to Mr Truesdale to prevent mistakes. That is to say I mean only to allow himself & family, servants excepted, to sit in Church times in the Chancel, & the same for his servants in the Brackenbury Chapel, but nothing there mentioned is to give him a power to alter, repair or strike a nail in any part of either, or any other power or liberty whatsoever. This I desire you will take particular case of, & if the words can be explained to give further liberty send me another article, properly worded, to execute, & cancel this, for in this point I will run no hazard.

Having had so much trouble already to bring this to bear I beg it may
stand clear of any new Treaty, & that he may execute as I have done, after which if he desires a new agreement for the rest he shall have them altogether:
Remainder of Trenleys, as you set it, at £16.0.0 Hovels at £20.0.0
Hills at £30.0.0
The timber to be valued by one or two persons to be named, the price 30 years purchase, but pray let him sign & seal before a word is said of this.

I mentioned before the goods I mean to reserve. He is to have only what is, strictly speaking, fixtures. Thank you for writing about Brentwood. I must send you the paper in my next letter about the fishery. I have no time, being now on the point of setting out for Leicester, to say more than
Yours
R N
Plymouth October 17th 1762
My Dearest Sophie

I was going as I promised to attempt to describe to you Mount Edgecombe but as I can always speak best with my pencil I have scratched out a map of the situation, which is one of the most magnificent I ever beheld, as you may judge by the sketch I send you, & I assure you I have introduced very little more than what you command from the Park & House.

Palmer & I took our horses on Friday & rode to the Town of Dock, 2 miles, & to the passage which I have marked. From thence we sailed to Lord Edgcombes gates & walked over a fine lawn to the house, which is about halfway up the hill. The stone of this country is too hard & rough to work to a truth, as we masons say. Its colour too, which is a reddish black. being all really marble mixed with a very white lime, is not agreeable to the eye, & the house being old, with 4 octagons newly added to the angles, makes a better appearance at a distance than near. The inside too is very indifferent, & has nothing worth seeing but some fine
marble pillars in the hall, which are cut out of the hill itself, & take a fine polish.

The gardener not being in the way we scrambled up to the highest part of the park, which is full of plantations but too bleak for them to prosper. We went near Maker Church & then turned south, down the hill to a stile which introduced us into the plantation, along the cliff & to one of the most agreeable walks I ever saw. The sun shone upon the unbounded ocean which lay under us, chequerd with the shadows of the clouds as they passed, & we seemed as far from the resort of Man as if the country was desert, till two large vessels came in full sail from the East Point, under the new house, & drew us on to the busy scene which this town of war & trade exhibits on every side. Everything on that side seemed in motion.

In one part of the cliff walk an awkward arch is built, throe which you see the Eddistone as a termination. The garden disappointed me, a few scattered myrtles grow bushwise about but look very unthriving. There are two hedges of the same, about two feet high, some magnolias, one lemon & an orange or two not much higher look miserably, & I could discover the marks of shelter applied to them in the winter. The winds are very bleak & I was surprised to find all the oranges housed. They are in tubs &, I think, the finest plants I ever saw, brought from Genoa a few years ago, the stems eight feet high, clear & beautiful, the heads not 4 feet round, but if they ever grow in proportion to the stems they will be very extraordinary. The taste of gardening as well as building here runs very low. Nature has left no room for improvement here, planting excepted, which is well done.

I will now leave you to my drawing, only add the colouring which the sun gave it, & I can't. But remember the verdure of the hills & enclosures. Park & lawns very fine, the tops of the cliffs & quarries red, their feet black with the beating of the waves, the houses rough stone, much limed, whitish, their roofs of slate, blue, the ships some with flags out, some in full sail, the water everywhere chequered with little boats & sloops, & varying its colours to the sun & clouds. Nothing could be more beautiful. I longed for you to see it. All I can do is to describe it.

Now I must tell you, Madam, this is the last letter I shall honour you with. Perhaps, please God, I may be with you before this letter . Hard luck indeed if I am not before another could. Tomorrow for the first time I am Field Officer of the Day. At noon I take a walk & visit the prisons. That's all my business except wearing a sash & gorget. Whaler is gone to day to Bath. His uncle there is dead & has left him all he has. You may see my walk for tomorrow in the Plan, where I have marked all the prisons. Hay has resigned upon a bullying letter of the Colonel. Says his
Commission is taken from him. He paid Dadley for doing his duty. Now the Corps must suffer for the vacancy. This is all.
November 25th 1762 Spring Garden

I kiss my dearest Sophys pale... I came safe & without the least accident at 10 o'clock this morning, & immediately marched to Cocoa to breakfast to learn news. As I came back to dress looked into the Mews where were more than 200 people, I believe, gathered round the Coachhouse doors to have the first sight of the State Coach. It was then 11 o'clock & they were to wait till near one. At half past 12 I went in a chair with great difficulty to the House, for such was the eagerness of all ranks to see the show that every street & alley was full, & though they permitted his Majesty to go down, they made him wait above an hour in Palace Yard, & at last were forced to drive all the coaches that filled the streets into the Park to make room for him to return, which was not accomplished till past 4.

Many of the Members, amongst them Bagot, Sir Charles Mordant etc could not get down to the House. Lord Bute , some say, was mob'd & insulted, & some incivilities went higher, No Scotchm-n, Newcastle for ever' etc. That noble Duke began with a mob & seems determined to end with one, for they say it was not only curiosity to see the Coach that drew together such a concourse. I send you the Speech; the Address is the echo to it. It was moved by Lord Carysford, seconded by Lord Charles Spencer. There was a peculiar gravity & piety in the Motion that moved up Mr Calvert who said he could make the House laugh, & he did so by accusing the noble lord of having stole his speech from the Preface to 4 Sermons published by William Fleetwood, Bishop of St Asaph at the time of making the Peace of Utrecht, but said he had misquoted & repeated the passage. The truth is his Lordship had altered the passage which you will find in Boyer's Oueen Anne, 1713. The Prelate set up the Whigs' standard & his sermons were burnt by the
Hangman, by order of her last Parliament. He displayed the wonderful successes of that war down to the period of the Treaty, then stops & adds,
Our enemies will tell the rest with pleasure'.

Lord Carysford stole the first part, but the last would not fit him, so he altered it. A thorough roasting . He stood for it for a considerable time. Nothing was said in opposition. The Lord Mayor called it an innocent address & said that if the Preliminaries are as they were printed in the papers he would undertake to prove them inadequate to our victories, insecure & inglorious.

Charles Townsend answered him with spirit; said he had the honour to descend from a person whose glory it was to have been voted an enemy to his country by that Parliament that made the Treaty of Utrecht, & if this was like that he would have showed his blood was genuine, but believed it very different. This was all we had of consequence. The Address passed name con .
In the Lords Lord Egmont & - I forget who -, moved the Address. Lord Aylesford & Lord Northumberland moved an Address to the Queen on the birth. We have lumped that in ours...
Now for conjectures.

The struggle, they say, is whether Grenville or Newcastle shall be King . Both master the Houses. The last, they say themselves, have 120. Mr Fox, who is very gracious to us, says only 75 Commons & 42 Lords, 8 of whom are Bishops. They are not to oppose the Preliminaries, which are expected in the next week, but to attack Lord Bute in every shape. 8 of them were to have thrown up yesterday when they went in a body to the Leve`e , but thought better of it, the King having declared that no man that gives up now shall ever come in again, & they say they would not give his Majesty the uneasiness to break his word as they are sure he must take them again. So resignations are stopped & I conclude from thence their opposition will be shortlived.

The Country Gentlemen, I believe, will be unanimous. That is a blow they will feel, & if they let the Preliminaries be approved by Parliament, if I was the Minister, I should care little for them afterwards. There is great confusion but Lord Bute seems to be very firm, goes on his way & keeps his object steadily in view & probably, I think, will attain it.

The speech promises reductions. Denbigh says the Militia will be immediately in part disembodied after the ratifications come over, those who are in their Counties & not on duty first, others not till the Peace is concluded amongst which he reckons ours, which will stay perhaps 2 months more where they are. For this he quotes Lord Ligonier.

The papers say Miss Pakington is dead. How sudden & surprising! I
shall consult Telly about mourning. The Bell will not let me read nor finish my letter...
